![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14274523/assets/276497b6f3ed88f51e3b08eef008ac5e2340748b73628d187d90c750ca68684e.png)

Consider all possible circular sectors $MON$ with perimeter $P=1$ units. What is the largest possible area $A$ of the circular sectors?
questions.worked_solution:
First,  let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta $ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $1$ unit, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
1=2r+r\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\theta =\frac{1-2r}{r}=\frac{1}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{1}{r}-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=\frac{1}{2}-2r.
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}-2r & =0 \\ r & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we confirm that $r=\frac{1}{4}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(\frac{1}{4})=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(\frac{1}{4})$ is negative, we conclude that $r=\frac{1}{4}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Therefore, the circular sector of the largest area will have a radius of $\frac{1}{4}$, and the area is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4})-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider all circular sectors $MON$ with area $A=100$ square units. Determine the angle $\theta $ (in radians) of the circular sector that has the smallest possible perimeter. Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}  radians
questions.worked_solution:
We let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta $ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. Then, we want to minimize the perimeter

$$
P=2r+r\theta .
$$

We know that the area is fixed at $100$ square units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
100=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation and taking into account that $r>0,$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta  \\ \theta  & =\frac{200}{{r}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging this into our expression for $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =2r+r\theta  \\  & =2r+r\cdot \frac{200}{{r}^{2}} \\  & =2r+\frac{200}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $P,$ so we need to differentiate $P$ and set the derivative equal to zero. Computing the derivative gives 

$$
{P}^{′}(r)=2-\frac{200}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{200}{{r}^{2}} & =0 \\ 2{r}^{2} & =200 \\ {r}^{2} & =100 \\ r & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we confirm that $r=10$ is a minimum using the second derivative test.

Since the second derivative ${P}^{″}(r)=\frac{400}{{r}^{3}}>0,$ the stationary point $r=10$ is a minimum. 

Finally, when $r=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\frac{200}{{r}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{200}{100} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

A contractor wants to design an entrance sign made up of a rectangle topped by a semicircle, as shown in the diagram. The area of the sign must be $100\,{cm}^{2}.$ What should be the radius $r$ of the semicircle so that the perimeter of the sign is minimized? Do not round the answer.

$r=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{cm}$
questions.worked_solution:
We let $r$ be the radius of the semicircle and let $x$ be the height of the rectangle. Then, we want to minimize the perimeter

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =2x+2r+\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the area is fixed at $100\text{ cm},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
100=2rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Now, by making $2x$ the subject of the constraint equation and taking into account that $r>0,$ we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =2rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2} \\ 2rx & =100-\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2} \\ 2x & =\frac{100}{r}-\frac{\pi r}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging this into our expression for $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\frac{100}{r}-\frac{\pi r}{2}+2r+\pi r \\  & =\frac{100}{r}+\frac{\pi r}{2}+2r.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $P,$ so we need to differentiate $P$ and set the derivative equal to zero. Computing the derivative gives

$$
{P}^{′}(r)=-\frac{100}{{r}^{2}}+\frac{\pi }{2}+2.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{100}{{r}^{2}}+\frac{\pi }{2}+2 & =0 \\ \frac{100}{{r}^{2}} & =\frac{\pi +4}{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{200}{\pi +4} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{200}{\pi +4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=\sqrt{\frac{200}{\pi +4}}$ is a minimum using the second derivative test.

Since the second derivative ${P}^{″}(r)=\frac{200}{{r}^{3}}>0,$ the stationary point 
$r=\sqrt{\frac{200}{\pi +4}}$ is a minimum.
